name: Omar Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you do on a normal factory day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, 43, and I lead the aluminium extrusion press that makes long window-frame sections. I hold a two-year technical diploma, and I can tell from the first cut whether a die is pulling the metal to one side. The good part is a frame that slots in without filing; the bad part is cleaning a jam when the press is still warm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do work and money sit with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Salma works at a child-care centre, and our two children are still in school. The mortgage and their bus fare come out of my ordinary lead wage and her smaller pay packet, with about three months of expenses saved. There are some other metal shops nearby, but I would need to see their actual shifts. I have never used AI tools; I trust a caliper and the die log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can print a neater order list, but an aluminium window frame still has to fit the gauge. The press and the people beside it would carry on much as they do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages cover the mortgage, and three months saved gives us time if a machine is down. The small AI shortcut would not threaten my paid hours, although I still watch the cost of the children's bus tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the extrusion press and measure the first frame after every die change. If the plant offers one extra paid Saturday each month, I would put part of that new wage into the household reserve after the mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job. I do not need an AI screen to tell me a frame is twisted, and I can carry on teaching the newer operators the physical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a new operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lay the first frame on a flat table and run a caliper across both sides. Last month that caught a thin corner before a whole rack went to packing. A window frame can look straight until the installer tries to fit the glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Saturday work is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not add anything from it to savings. The regular wage covers our current bills, but an extra shift on a noticeboard is not money until it is paid.

say: I would say **window frames** still need physical measurements despite tidier orders.
I would show new operators the **first-cut check** before a rack reaches packing.
think: Our **regular wages** and three-month reserve cover the mortgage in this quiet picture.
An **extra Saturday** would help savings only if the plant actually pays it.
do: **Keep** running the extrusion press and gauging the first frame after each die change.
**Save** part of an offered paid Saturday wage after ordinary bills.
feel: **Calm** about my current hours and the family's workable budget.
S0.quote: A window frame can look straight until the installer tries to fit the glass.
fieldNote: His **caliper check** catches defects after a die change, while the small office shortcut leaves physical press work intact.
The **new reserve deposit** depends on an actual extra paid Saturday; the three months already saved are a buffer.

steps.text: Keep pressing window frames and measuring first cuts after die changes
Save part of paid extra Saturday wage after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop that AI may plan metal orders and write schedules before robots can change a hot die. I would ask for the paid roster on paper before somebody claims the press needs fewer hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first-cut skill still matters, but a tighter schedule could remove one of my regular changeover shifts. Salma's child-care wage would not fill that hole, and three months saved would run down quickly. I do not like a system that changes pay without a person explaining it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the next posted roster with my last four pay slips and keep making the first-cut checks. If the plant requires a new guarded-die course and offers a paid trainer-led place on a stopped press, I would take it. If my base hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted nearby metal-shop jobs whose safe duties, base wage and school-compatible shift cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible short wage, even while I know the press well. I want a written number, not a cheerful promise from a supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the die course have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would have to show me how to isolate the ram, lock the die and check the first extrusion with the guard closed. I would not reach across a moving press for a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which wage figure matters on another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the guaranteed base rate, not a possible overtime total, with the mortgage and school bus fares. A longer commute that loses the children's pickup would not help us.

say: I would ask for a **written base roster** before accepting a faster press target.
A **paid guarded course** must use a stopped press and a real trainer.
think: A shorter **changeover roster** could cut my own pay.
Salma's **child-care wage** and three months saved cannot replace a regular factory shift for long.
do: **Compare** posted base shifts with four actual pay slips.
**Take** required die-change instruction only if a paid safe trainer-led place is offered.
**Apply** after real cuts only to posted nearby safe metal work at bill-covering pay and workable hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible loss of regular hours despite my strong press skill.
S1.quote: I would not reach across a moving press for a certificate.
fieldNote: He seeks **real roster evidence** before treating scheduling software as a wage cut, but has a concrete search if hours fall.
His **resistance to AI** does not prevent required practical training when paid and taught safely on a stopped press.

steps.text: Compare posted extrusion roster with four pay slips
Take guarded die course if required paid stopped-press trainer place offered
Apply after base-hour cuts to posted safe nearby metal jobs if pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Salma that AGI could plan the window-frame orders in 2028, while capable robots that change dies and clear the press follow around 2031. I would want the owner to put remaining paid jobs and dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our press shifts to go when robots can change dies and inspect frames without us. My lead title would not guarantee one of the few remaining jobs. Three months saved and Salma's smaller wage would not cover the mortgage for long; I would lie awake over the next school payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the kitchen refit before paying its deposit and keep that cash for bills. If a funded paid course in frame-strength testing offers a guarded practical place, I would attend; after qualifying, if my hours are cut, I would apply for a posted safe local testing job only if its base pay and shift cover our mortgage and the children's care. If the course is not offered, I would apply for posted nearby production work under those same pay, safety and school-hour terms while keeping any press wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a likely large loss of pay. I can look for work, but I cannot use a course leaflet to pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test in a practical class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the frame wall thickness, break a bad sample and stop the press before anyone touches a die. A trainer would have to watch the isolation on a guarded machine; I cannot pay for an unsafe shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower paid production job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the guaranteed wage still meets our mortgage, food and child-care costs without assumed overtime. I would need a posted shift that lets one of us collect the children, not a title on a noticeboard.

say: I would distinguish **2028 order planning** from physical press robots around 2031.
I would ask the owner for **written paid-job dates** before the crew is cut.
think: I expect **most press shifts** to disappear once robots can change dies.
Three months of **savings** and Salma's wage cannot carry our mortgage for long.
do: **Cancel** the kitchen refit before its deposit to preserve bill money.
**Take** funded paid guarded frame testing only if a practical place is offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local testing if qualified and cut, or production work if no course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless school-cost worry.
S2.quote: I can look for work, but I cannot use a course leaflet to pay the mortgage.
fieldNote: His **physical press work** faces capable robots around 2031; 2028 AGI first changes order planning.
The **testing route** needs a funded paid safe place and qualification; the independent production fallback needs real safe postings and adequate hours.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen refit before deposit and keep cash for bills
Take frame-strength course if funded paid guarded trainer place offered
Apply for posted safe local testing if qualified and cut, base pay and pickup fit
Apply for posted safe nearby production if no course, base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan aluminium orders in 2031, and capable robots might change the dies around 2034. Five years is enough to judge a real training offer, provided the factory keeps the wage coming while people learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when capable robots reach the press. My diploma and years as lead could help me inspect frames, but there might be fewer paid inspection jobs than press operators. The mortgage would still need a reliable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an offered extra paid shift in busy months and add part of that new pay to a reserve after bills. I would enroll in a recognised materials-inspection course only if the employer pays the fee and release time and provides guarded practice with a trainer. After passing, if press hours fall, I would apply for a posted safe local inspector role only if its base pay and shift fit our mortgage and school pickup; without a workable course, I would look for posted nearby press work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though there is time to read the course terms properly. I would rather keep a real press shift than buy a badge with no posted job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show you the inspector course is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to bend a weak sample, measure the wall and record a rejection beside a qualified inspector. The course needs an actual seat on paid time, not just a brochure with a laboratory picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you assess the inspector posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the plant address, base wage and exact shift start. Some shops are nearby, but a long journey and a lower rate could erase the benefit of a new title.

say: I would require **paid practical inspection** before robots reach the press around 2034.
An **inspector vacancy** needs a posted rate and usable hours.
think: My **diploma and experience** might help, but inspection places could be scarce.
The **mortgage** still needs paid work if physical press jobs narrow.
do: **Save** part of newly paid busy-month shifts after ordinary bills.
**Enroll** in recognised inspection only with employer-paid fee, release and guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted safe local inspection, or press work if no course, at workable pay.
feel: **Anxious** about eventual hours, with time to check real wages and instruction.
S3.quote: I would rather keep a real press shift than buy a badge with no posted job behind it.
fieldNote: He is willing to learn **materials inspection** only with covered fees, paid release and guarded hands-on assessment.
Both the qualified **inspection move** and no-course press fallback depend on actual safe local posts, sufficient base pay and school pickup.

steps.text: Save part of new paid busy-month shifts after bills
Enroll in recognised inspection if fee and release paid and guarded trainer place offered
Apply for posted safe inspector if qualified and cut, base pay and pickup fit
Search posted safe nearby press work if no course, base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop that AGI may plan aluminium orders in 2036, while capable robots might do the die change around 2039. A decade is time to put training and paid posts on paper, not to pretend the press will stay exactly as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when capable robots reach the machine. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is finished or Salma's child-care hours unchanged. Our current regular wages and three-month reserve let us plan without an immediate loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the press and pay extra mortgage principal from newly paid overtime after ordinary bills. I would ask the employer each year for actual course places and posted inspector rates, then take a recognised guarded course only if fees, paid release and a trainer are supplied. If robots later cut press hours, I would apply after qualifying only for posted safe local inspection work whose base wage and shift cover our remaining bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, while the wage we have now is sound. I want to look at real posts before I ask the family to change anything large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots reach the press?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the pension figures and our mortgage balance before deciding when to stop. If they do not cover the bills, I would continue seeking paid work; a date on a calendar is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe inspection offer include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the posted base rate, a shift Salma and I can manage, and the authority to stop a weak frame before packing. An inspection title without a stop button is just blame with a badge.

say: I would ask for **real paid posts** before the press changes around 2039.
The **2036 planning date** gives time to check training terms before physical robots arrive.
think: At **56**, I may still need the press wage for the mortgage.
Our current **two-wage household** and three-month reserve make the nearer years manageable.
do: **Pay** extra mortgage principal only from newly paid overtime after bills.
**Take** recognised inspection training if fees, paid release and guarded trainer practice are offered.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts only to posted safe local work at bill-covering base pay and workable hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant press jobs while our present wages remain reliable.
S4.quote: An inspection title without a stop button is just blame with a badge.
fieldNote: He checks **annual course places** and written wages before training, and treats pension figures as information rather than an exit decision.
Extra **mortgage payments** require newly paid overtime; any later inspection job needs qualification, cut hours and suitable posted pay.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from newly paid overtime after bills
Ask employer yearly for actual course places and posted inspector rates
Take recognised guarded inspection course if fees and release paid and trainer place offered
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified and cut, base pay and shift fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take most extrusion-press shifts before our mortgage is smaller. Written staffing dates, a funded paid guarded course and posted safe local jobs with enough base pay would help. I would check the shift times with Salma before applying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the first window frame after a robot changes the die. I can show an apprentice the thin corner in ten seconds with a caliper. A stack of straight-looking frames is no use if none of them fits the glass.

headlineQuote: A stack of straight-looking frames is no use if none of them fits the glass.
portrait: **Omar**, 43, leads an aluminium window-frame press and holds a two-year technical diploma earned for machine work.
He and **child-care worker** Salma support two school-age children and a mortgage on typical lead pay with three months saved.
He has **never used AI** and judges changes by caliper results, actual rosters, paid trainers and safe die practice.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm him about most press shifts; longer warnings let him inspect funded courses and posted jobs before moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable extrusion robots around 2031 and remove the wages covering his mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written staffing dates**, paid guarded instruction and posted safe local work with a base wage his family can use.
